opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing to say is that you have to be careful about which trend you extrapolate. If you look at benchmark performance on things like coding or math competitions, progress looks extremely fast, and it's tempting to draw a line and say we'll have automated most remote work in a couple of years. But I don't think those benchmarks are measuring the thing that's actually the bottleneck.

When I look at what remote workers actually do all day, it's not mostly solving well-specified, self-contained problems. It's managing context over weeks or months, coordinating with other people, noticing when something's gone wrong without being told, deciding what to work on, and executing long sequences of actions where small errors compound. The models we have are very impressive at the short-horizon, crisply defined stuff, and much weaker at exactly those agentic, long-horizon capabilities. That's a kind of Moravec's paradox: the things we found hard, like competition math, turned out to be relatively easy, and the things we take for granted, like just competently doing a job end to end, turned out to be hard.

So the way I'd frame it is: rather than extrapolating benchmark scores, look at how much of the economy AI is actually doing. Revenue from AI is growing fast, but it's still a tiny fraction of the total value of remote work, which is trillions of dollars a year. If these systems were close to being drop-in remote workers, you'd expect to see much more economic impact than we do.

Then the other way to think about it is in terms of inputs. A lot of the progress over the past decade has come from scaling compute, roughly several-fold per year in training runs, plus algorithmic improvements. Each big unlock, from reasoning to agency, seems to require something like additional orders of magnitude of effective compute. That scaling can't continue at the current pace indefinitely; at some point you run into limits on chip production, energy, and how much money people are willing to spend. So there's a window this decade where we're climbing through a lot of orders of magnitude very quickly, and if full automation of remote work doesn't arrive within that window, progress likely slows down, because we'd be relying more on algorithmic progress and slower hardware growth.

Putting that together, I'm more skeptical than many people in the Bay Area of timelines like two or three years. My median for something like fully automating remote work would be more on the order of a couple of decades, maybe in the 2040s, with substantial uncertainty in both directions. I don't think it's crazy that it happens sooner, but I think people are over-updating on impressive demos and benchmarks and under-updating on how much of real work is the messy, long-horizon, context-heavy stuff that these systems still struggle with.

r001.rationale: The response says AI revenue is still a tiny fraction of remote-work value, but it does not extrapolate that fraction to suggest centuries until full automation.

r002.rationale: It describes capabilities still lacking and progress over the past decade, but does not propose comparing those acquired and remaining capabilities to assess prospects for broad economic transformation.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that you can't extrapolate it cleanly from the recent progress, because the thing you'd want to extrapolate isn't really one trend. People look at the benchmarks and see this very steep curve, and the natural move is to say, well, if it keeps going at this slope, then in a couple of years it's done. But the benchmarks are measuring a fairly narrow slice of what remote work actually is. They're measuring things like, can you solve this math problem, can you fix this bug in this repository given a clean description of it. And that's real progress, I don't want to dismiss it. But the capabilities that are missing for full automation are not just a slightly harder version of that. They're things like long-horizon coherence, being able to work on something for weeks where the goal is kind of vague and shifts over time, and learning on the job, where you go into a company and after six months you're much more useful than you were on day one because you've picked up a lot of tacit context. And current systems basically don't do that at all. So on those dimensions the trend line is much less clear, because we haven't really been measuring them until very recently.

The way I'd frame it is more like, there's a set of things you need, and we've been knocking out some of them quickly, and the remaining ones might be fast or might be slow. If you look at the history of AI there's been a pattern where the stuff that looked hard turned out to be easy and the stuff that looked easy, like reliably operating in a messy environment for a long time, turned out to be hard. And I think that should make you somewhat humble about the extrapolation.

Where that leaves me is, I put real probability on it happening within, say, the next decade, but my median is further out than what a lot of people in San Francisco would say. And a big reason for that is just the scale of what's being claimed. Fully automating remote work is not a modest claim. It's essentially saying you've got a drop-in replacement for the entire cognitive workforce, and the economic consequences of that would be enormous, way beyond anything we've seen. So before I believe we're two or three years away from something that dramatic, I'd want to see more than benchmark progress. I'd want to see the systems actually being deployed in a way that's generating a lot of economic value, and right now, compared to what the capabilities would seem to suggest, that's still fairly limited. That gap itself is informative. It tells you there's something about real work that the benchmarks aren't capturing.

r001.rationale: The response does not estimate automation by the fraction of the economy automated or suggest that extrapolating it implies centuries to full automation.

r002.rationale: It contrasts recent benchmark progress with remaining capabilities, but does not compare those capabilities with what AI acquired over the past 10–15 years.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between progress on the things we can measure and progress toward actually doing somebody’s job. Those are related, but they’re not the same thing. A model can get much better at coding benchmarks without being able to take over the job of a software engineer, because the job involves figuring out what to do, getting context from other people, and checking whether what you’ve done actually solves the problem.

So I would put more weight on the length and complexity of tasks that models can complete reliably, with little human intervention. Can they do something that takes a person an hour? A day? A week? If that keeps increasing quickly, that’s much stronger evidence for remote work being automated than another jump in a benchmark score.

But even there, extrapolation is tricky. A weeklong task isn’t necessarily just a lot of short tasks chained together. You might need to notice that your initial approach is wrong, or ask somebody a question you didn’t know you needed to ask. Whether those difficulties get resolved smoothly as models improve is a big uncertainty.

Recent progress makes relatively short timelines plausible to me. I just wouldn’t infer a precise date for full automation from it. Automating a substantial fraction of remote work and automating essentially all of it are quite different thresholds.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts benchmark gains with job automation and discusses task-length extrapolation, but it does not say that extrapolating the fraction of the economy automated could imply centuries to full automation.

r002.rationale: The response discusses capabilities needed to complete real jobs, but it does not compare those capabilities with what AI acquired over the past 10–15 years.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to distinguish between progress on tasks we can measure and progress toward doing an entire job. We’ve seen very rapid progress on things like coding benchmarks and answering difficult questions. But a remote worker has to do much more than produce a good answer to a well-specified question. They have to figure out what needs doing, gather context, interact with other people, and notice when something has gone wrong.

So I’m wary of taking a benchmark trend and extrapolating it directly to a date for full automation. The trend is evidence that the underlying capabilities are improving quickly. It doesn’t tell you, by itself, how reliably those capabilities will translate into work over a week or a month.

One thing I’d look at is how long a task an AI can complete autonomously at a given level of reliability. If that horizon keeps increasing rapidly on realistic tasks, that would be much stronger evidence for short timelines. But you also have to ask whether the tasks are representative. A coding problem with a clear test suite is different from being told, ‘Our customers are unhappy—figure out why and fix it.’

And ‘fully automate remote work’ is a very demanding endpoint. You could have enormous economic effects well before that, with systems doing a large fraction of the work while humans supply direction and handle exceptions. I’d put more confidence in continued rapid expansion of what can be automated than in any particular date when the whole category is finished.

r001.rationale: The response cautions against extrapolating benchmark trends to a date for full automation, but does not say that extrapolating the economy’s automated share could imply centuries.

r002.rationale: It discusses capabilities still needed for whole jobs, but does not compare them with capabilities AI has gained over the past 10–15 years.
